text: A simple chat turn is one round trip: you send a message, the model replies, and it's done. An agent is the same kind of model, given tools to call and permission to keep running in a loop instead of stopping after one reply.

In plain chat, the model writes one reply and the conversation waits for you again. In an agent, the model decides an action, a tool runs, the model sees the result, and it decides the next action itself — looping until it decides the goal is actually done.

Take a policy question a model can't answer from memory alone. A pure chat model guesses or admits it doesn't know. An agent with a document search tool calls that tool first, reads the real policy text back, and only then answers — and if the first search misses, it can try again, because it hasn't stopped running yet.

Agency isn't all or nothing. A system that calls one tool and stops is more agentic than plain chat but far simpler than one that loops for many steps, reflects on its own output, and coordinates other agents — and more agency isn't automatically better, which is exactly why a later lesson is devoted to when agents are overkill.

The core shift is simple to state: a model that gets to take more than one step toward an answer, checking its own work against the real world along the way. Next up: what that loop actually looks like, step by step.
